proposals.relationship: May identifies Gordon’s women’s-history scholarship as an influence on her early research and her understanding of the connections between public and private life.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2025 retrospective explicitly names Gordon among a plural peer cohort and cites Woman’s Body, Woman’s Right (1976) in note 7. This is May’s later recollection, not proof that a 1976 book shaped her 1975 degree work. The cited original is unread. Gordon is a peer/inspiration here, not an inferred formal supervisor. May also gives world events a larger role in prompting her questions.
primary_locators: H-Diplo Essay E619, 6 March 2025, PDF p. 4 paragraph beginning Social history was new and n. 7; PDF p. 5 paragraph beginning Ultimately.

proposals.relationship: May credits Kerber’s women’s-history scholarship as an early research influence and uses republican motherhood to explain the older civic lineage of Cold War domestic ideals.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2025 retrospective names Kerber in a plural cohort and note 7 cites Women of the Republic (1980); own 2008 Homeward Bound p. 98 explicitly uses her argument on mothers as educators of citizens before distinguishing the space-age version. No 1980-to-1975 causal chronology, sole-source claim or formal mentorship inferred. Complete Kerber original and Homeward Bound endnote 28 remain unread.
primary_locators: 2025 E619 PDF p. 4/n. 7 and p. 5 Ultimately paragraph; Homeward Bound 2008 printed pp. 98–99, paragraph beginning The ideological connections through contrast with Victorian mothers, note-call 28.

proposals.relationship: May draws on Roediger’s account of Irish immigrants’ pursuit of whiteness when explaining changing racial boundaries and postwar mobility.
proposals.evidence_note: Own PBS answer explicitly credits Roediger, then differentiates later immigrant cohorts and enduring exclusions. The interview does not identify which Roediger work or edition; no title is guessed and no original book is newly read. This extends the source’s previously checked employment/family passages with an explicit named conceptual resource.
primary_locators: PBS Tupperware interview, answer to How did American attitudes toward ethnic groups change during and after the war?, opening Irish-immigration paragraph and following postwar contrast.

proposals.relationship: May’s review endorses Cott’s account of marriage law as a constitutive part of citizenship, racial and gender hierarchy, and national policy.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 2001 signed review’s two-paragraph publisher extract supplies substantive named reception. It records May’s acceptance of an argument in that review, not formative influence on her earlier books or proof that the entire review is uniformly favorable. Cott’s 2000 Public Vows and the remainder of May’s pp. 1046–1047 review are unread.
primary_locators: Journal of American History 88:3 (December 2001), 1046–1047, publisher Extract: opening paragraph Nancy F. Cott’s sweeping history through reproduction; following paragraph Public Vows traces through marital model.
